sections.text:
1 cod. μηχεία. 2 cod. γιτόνων. 3 ἀνεβλαβῆς cod., ἄνευ βλάβης scripsimus.
6 ἔσεσθαι cod., ἔσται scripsimus. 10 συγκλειτικῶν cod., συγκλητικῶν scripsimus.
11 τούτους cod., τούτοις Boll. cod. συνεναίσαντες. 12 εἰς = ἐν Boll. · ὥστε >
Boll. 13 αὐτὸν ξίφοι cod., αὐτῷ ξίφει Boll. 14 cod. ἰσμαηλεῖται. 15 cod. ἀλλήλ-
λων. cod. φυγεῖν τραπήσεται ξυχεία cod., φυγὴν τραπήσονται ὀξεῖαν scripsimus.
16 cod. κουμανοία. Sunt Turci Cumani qui ripam Ponti Euxini incolebant (Cumont).
Num Ἀλβανία in Caucaso? Etsi Alanorum nomen etiam extremis Byzantini imperii
temporibus comparet. 17 cod. καὶ ἀβασίλευτοι delevimus καὶ. cod. (post ἔσον-
ται) ὑπὸ τοῦ ξάνθου · καίπερ οὐ ἔθνη διωκόμενοι quae correcta suo loco posuimus.
19 cod. αἰγόκερος. cod. ἄμειναν. 20 cod. μειχανοῖς. 21 cod. τῶν τόπων.
22 μικρὰ cod., μακρὰ scripsimus. cod. αὐτοῖς.
sections.en: 1 the codex has μηχεία ('adultery'). 2 the codex has γιτόνων ('of neighbors'). 3 ἀνεβλαβῆς ('unharmed') the codex has, ἄνευ βλάβης ('without harm') we have written. 6 ἔσεσθαι ('to be') the codex has, ἔσται ('will be') we have written. 10 συγκλειτικῶν ('of senators') the codex has, συγκλητικῶν ('of senators') we have written. 11 τούτους ('these') the codex has, τούτοις ('to these') Boll. the codex has συνεναίσαντες ('dwelling together'). 12 εἰς ('into') = ἐν ('in') Boll. · ὥστε ('so that') > Boll. 13 αὐτὸν ξίφοι ('him with a sword') the codex has, αὐτῷ ξίφει ('him with a sword') Boll. 14 the codex has ἰσμαηλεῖται ('Ishmaelites'). 15 the codex has ἀλλήλλων ('of one another'). the codex has φυγεῖν τραπήσεται ξυχεία ('will turn to flee swiftly') the codex has, φυγὴν τραπήσονται ὀξεῖαν ('they will turn to swift flight') we have written. 16 the codex has κουμανοία ('Cumania'). They are the Cuman Turks who inhabited the bank of the Euxine Sea (Cumont). Is it Ἀλβανία ('Albania') in the Caucasus? Although the name of the Alans appears even in the last times of the Byzantine empire. 17 the codex has καὶ ἀβασίλευτοι ('and without a king') we have deleted καὶ ('and'). the codex has (after ἔσονται ('they will be')) ὑπὸ τοῦ ξάνθου · καίπερ οὐ ἔθνη διωκόμενοι ('by the yellow [river/man]; although not pursued by nations') which, corrected, we have placed in their own place. 19 the codex has αἰγόκερος ('Capricorn'). the codex has ἄμειναν ('they remained'). 20 the codex has μειχανοῖς ('machines'). 21 the codex has τῶν τόπων ('of the places'). 22 μικρὰ ('small') the codex has, μακρὰ ('long') we have written. the codex has αὐτοῖς ('to them').

sections.text:
1 Fortasse nomen proprium in κλῆρος latet (num ὁ Σκληρός i. e. Bardas ὁ Σκλη-
ρός, qui in Asia circa finem saec. X contra Basilium II pugnavit?). Utut de hoc
loco cogitandum est, ea profecto quae passim commemorantur, nempe barbaro-
rum (Selgiukidorum?) incursiones in Asiae provincias (28, 4; cf. 27, 9), Cumano-
rum sedes (28, 16), Bulgarorum clades et bella (29, 21; cf. 29, 3 [?]), iconoclastarum
denique devastationes, quarum vestigia adhuc conspicua erant (29, 15), huiusmodi
sunt ut plane persuadeant hanc scriptiunculam forma qua nunc legimus vix
saeculo X ex. aut XI in. recentiorem esse. — Cf. etiam ad 26, 22.
sections.en: 1 Perhaps a proper name lies hidden in κλῆρος ('lot') (is it ὁ Σκληρός ('Skleros'), i.e. Bardas ὁ Σκληρός ('Skleros'), who fought in Asia around the end of the 10th century against Basil II?). However this passage is to be considered, those things which are mentioned here and there, namely the incursions of the barbarians (Seljuks?) into the provinces of Asia (28, 4; cf. 27, 9), the settlements of the Cumans (28, 16), the disasters and wars of the Bulgarians (29, 21; cf. 29, 3 [?]), and finally the devastations of the iconoclasts, the traces of which were still visible (29, 15), are of such a kind that they clearly persuade that this short writing, in the form in which we now read it, is scarcely more recent than the end of the 10th century or the beginning of the 11th century. — Cf. also on 26, 22.

summary.headline: Sagittarius and Capricorn Omens
summary.text: Astrological omens for thunder and earthquakes in Sagittarius and Capricorn, predicting disturbances, harvests, famine, political upheaval, wars, and the destruction of Roman royal power. The text names Asia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Armenia, Persians, Ishmaelites, Cumania, Alania, senators, and Chaldean interpretations.
